title: Operation Sana: The 5th Corps Breaks East
content:
For three years, the ARBiH 5th Corps had fought one of the most desperate defensive campaigns of the Bosnian War. Encircled in the Bihać pocket in northwestern Bosnia, the formation had endured siege, starvation, and simultaneous pressure from VRS forces, the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and the rebel forces of Fikret Abdić's Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia. At times the pocket had seemed on the verge of collapse. In late 1994, a VRS-RSK-APWB offensive had nearly overrun the enclave entirely. The 5th Corps, under the command of General Atif Dudaković, held on through a combination of tactical resourcefulness, terrain advantage, and sheer determination.

In September 1995, everything changed. Operation Storm had destroyed the Republic of Serbian Krajina, eliminating the forces that had pressed the Bihać pocket from the west and north. NATO's Operation Deliberate Force was devastating VRS military infrastructure across Bosnia. The strategic encirclement that had defined the 5th Corps' existence for three years had been broken. Dudaković seized the moment.

Operation Sana sent the 5th Corps south and east in the largest ARBiH territorial advance of the entire war. The offensive was methodical and devastating. The 5th Corps captured Bosanska Krupa, Bosanski Petrovac, and Ključ in rapid succession as VRS defences collapsed across the region. On 11 October, Sanski Most — a town whose Bosniak population had been subjected to systematic persecution and expulsion in 1992, as documented in the ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T) — was liberated. The 5th Corps, which had spent the war's first three years fighting for survival in the most isolated pocket in Bosnia, was now spearheading a broad offensive that was reshaping the map.

The VRS 1st Krajina Corps, the largest formation in the Bosnian Serb army, could not contain the advance. Its units were depleted by three years of war, demoralized by the collapse of the Krajina Serb entity, battered by NATO air strikes, and stretched impossibly thin across a front that was expanding as Croatian forces simultaneously advanced from the south. The defensive positions that had held for years crumbled in days. Serb civilians fled eastward toward Banja Luka in large numbers, creating a humanitarian crisis that would become a factor in the diplomatic calculations driving the peace process.

The scale of the 5th Corps' advance was remarkable in context. An army that had been besieged, undersupplied, and outnumbered for most of the war captured more territory in three weeks than in any previous ARBiH campaign. The operation pushed Republika Srpska's western boundary eastward toward the approximate 49 percent territorial line that had been the basis of successive international peace proposals since the Contact Group plan of 1994.

Operation Sana also carried a dimension of return that was deeply significant for the Bosniak population. The towns captured by the 5th Corps had been the sites of some of the war's earliest ethnic cleansing campaigns. Sanski Most, Ključ, and Bosanski Petrovac had seen their Bosniak and Croat populations expelled through organized campaigns of violence and intimidation in the spring and summer of 1992. The 5th Corps' advance represented, at least symbolically, a reversal of those expulsions — though the reality of postwar return would prove far more complicated than any military operation could resolve.
